analysis.one_liner: Protects workers' wages, pensions, and union contracts when employers file bankruptcy, and bars executive bonus schemes in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in April 2025 with 6 cosponsors, including one Republican, and was referred to the Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company goes bankrupt, current law lets executives collect retention bonuses and performance pay while employees' unpaid wages and retirees' benefits are treated like ordinary debts and often trimmed. This bill doubles the amount of back wages workers get first in line from $10,000 to $20,000 and drops the 180-day cutoff for earning it, gives severance pay, benefit-plan contributions, and labor-law damages higher priority, and makes companies prove a union contract can only be rejected after genuine negotiations and as a last resort. It also blocks special bonus and incentive plans for executives, consultants, and top managers during a bankruptcy, and requires courts to weigh job preservation when approving asset sales or reorganization plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees of companies that file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy: they would recover more of their unpaid wages, severance, pension losses, and health benefits, and their union contracts would be much harder to void. Unions would gain standing and bargaining protections throughout the process.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees of bankrupt firms

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the priority wage claim cap from $10,000 to $20,000 per worker and removes the 180-day lookback and the business-closure cutoff, so more workers recover more of what they are owed ahead of unsecured creditors [S2][S3].

Gives higher priority to severance pay, contributions owed to employee benefit plans, back pay and penalties from labor-law violations including WARN Act mass-layoff damages, and pension plan withdrawal liabilities [S2][S3].

Rewrites the rules for rejecting union contracts: the company must keep paying under the contract, negotiate in good faith from a business plan, seek only the minimum savings essential to exit bankruptcy, and meet a clear-and-convincing court standard; if it has paid executives bonuses, courts must presume its cost-cutting burden on workers is disproportionate [S3].

Bars bonus, incentive, and retention payments to insiders, senior executives, the 20 highest-paid employees, division managers, and consultants unless the program applies generally to all full-time employees, tightens the pay-ratio limits, and allows the estate to claw back executive compensation when pensions or union benefits are cut [S2][S3].

Requires courts, when approving asset sales or reorganization plans, to favor buyers that preserve jobs, maintain wages and conditions, and assume pension and retiree health obligations, and requires a plan continuing the business to preserve going-concern value and jobs [S3].

Lets workers and retirees claim the shortfall in pension benefits when a plan is terminated, and claim losses in company stock held in 401(k)-type plans when the employer committed fraud or breached its duty [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Executives and consultants of bankrupt companies, who lose access to special retention and incentive pay schemes; secured lenders, whose collateral can be charged to cover unpaid employee wages and benefit contributions even when lenders waived such claims; and distressed-asset buyers, who can no longer buy companies free of jobs, pensions, and union obligations, and whose profitable liquidations and asset-stripping would be harder.

drawbacks.text: Restricting executive retention pay could push experienced turnaround managers away from distressed companies, and buyers required to keep jobs and pension obligations may bid less for failing businesses, reducing the cash available to pay all creditors [S3].

The bill shifts value from financial creditors toward employees, which banks and pension-plan investors would bear when companies fail, and it makes union contracts significantly harder to renegotiate, which could make lending to heavily unionized firms riskier [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and retirees facing a bankruptcy, the gains are direct and substantial: more recovered wages, protected severance and benefits, and real limits on the practice of paying executives bonuses while cutting retiree health or voiding union contracts. The tradeoff is real but narrower: distressed companies may be worth less to buyers and lenders when employee protections attach, which could mean fewer rescue deals and less creditor recovery in some cases. The bill targets a widely criticized asymmetry without touching healthy businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has not scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on April 9, 2025, joined by five cosponsors including Senator Hawley, a Republican [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary; the record shows no further action since [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote has been scheduled, and the Congress runs through January 2027 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bankruptcy attorneys and distressed-company advisors working within the current rules, and the executives and lenders the bill would restrict, are better off so far because the bill has not moved. Workers and retirees gain nothing until it advances.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Executives and lenders benefit from the status quo

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and set its terms: higher wage priority, union contract protections, and executive pay limits in bankruptcy [S1][S4].

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship [S4].

for.name: Sens. Schatz, Duckworth, Klobuchar, and Whitehouse

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 9, 2025 and has taken no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors are Democrats except Senator Hawley, a Republican, so the bill's support is bipartisan, though it is too early to know how the full Senate would split.

industries.industry: Executives, consultants, and turnaround specialists at distressed companies
industries.note: The bill bars their bonus, retention, and incentive pay schemes during bankruptcy unless the program applies to all employees, and lets the estate claw back compensation when worker benefits are cut. This ends a common practice of paying insiders while cutting retiree benefits.

Unpaid post-petition wages, vacation, severance, and benefit contributions would be charged against lenders' collateral even if the lenders had waived such charges. Lenders would also face less predictability in restructuring union-heavy companies.

Courts would have to favor buyers that preserve jobs, wages, and pension and retiree health obligations, making free-and-clear asset purchases and liquidation plays less attractive. Job preservation becomes part of the sale test.

industries.industry: Labor unions and multi-employer pension plans
industries.note: Unions gain notice, bargaining, and fee protections, a union right to file creditor claims, and an exception from the automatic stay for grievance and arbitration proceedings. Multi-employer plans get priority for withdrawal liability.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action since its April 2025 referral and no scheduled hearing, the bill is likely to sit in the Judiciary Committee and die when this Congress ends, as similar prior bankruptcy-reform bills have. Passage would require the committee to hold a markup and the full Senate to find floor time, neither of which is currently scheduled.
